questions.question: What is the primary reason SSDs are faster than HDDs for random reads?
options: SSDs use larger storage capacities
SSDs have no moving parts, eliminating mechanical seek time and rotational latency
SSDs compress data before storing it
SSDs use a faster version of the same magnetic technology
questions.explanation: HDDs rely on a mechanical arm that must physically move to the correct track (seek time) and then wait for the platter to rotate to the right sector (rotational latency). SSDs use electrical signals to access any cell directly, eliminating both mechanical delays.

questions.question: Why is sequential I/O significantly faster than random I/O on both HDDs and SSDs?
options: Sequential I/O uses a different file system than random I/O
Sequential I/O eliminates seek overhead on HDDs and enables prefetching and batching on SSDs
Sequential I/O bypasses the operating system entirely
Sequential I/O only works on newer hardware
questions.explanation: On HDDs, sequential reads avoid the costly mechanical seek between tracks. On SSDs, sequential access enables the controller to prefetch upcoming blocks and batch operations efficiently. Both the hardware and OS page cache are optimized for sequential access patterns.

questions.question: What is the page cache in an operating system?
options: A hardware component inside the SSD controller
A portion of RAM that the OS uses to cache recently accessed disk pages
A web browser feature for caching HTML pages
A special partition on the hard drive for swap space
questions.explanation: The page cache is a region of RAM managed by the OS kernel that stores recently read disk pages. When an application reads a file, the OS checks the page cache first. If the data is there (a cache hit), the disk is never touched, providing RAM-speed access to frequently used data.

questions.question: What is a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and what problem does it solve?
options: A log of all network requests, solving the problem of unauthorized access
A log where changes are recorded before being applied to the data file, solving crash recovery
A log of CPU instructions, solving the problem of slow execution
A user activity log for auditing purposes
questions.explanation: A Write-Ahead Log records intended changes to a sequential log file before those changes are applied to the actual data files. If the system crashes mid-write, the WAL can be replayed on startup to recover to a consistent state. This is the foundation of crash recovery in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and most databases.

questions.question: Why does a database server often perform poorly right after a restart but improve over time?
options: The CPU needs time to warm up its transistors
The page cache is cold after restart — frequently accessed data hasn't been loaded into RAM yet
The database needs to recompile all stored procedures
Network connections take time to stabilize
questions.explanation: After a restart, the OS page cache is empty (cold). Every data access must go to disk, which is orders of magnitude slower than RAM. As the server handles queries, frequently accessed pages accumulate in the cache (warm up), and subsequent reads hit RAM instead of disk.

questions.question: What role does the file system play between applications and raw disk storage?
options: It encrypts all data before writing to disk
It organizes data into files and directories, maps them to disk blocks, and manages metadata like permissions and timestamps
It compresses all files to save disk space
It converts all data to binary before storage
questions.explanation: The file system is an abstraction layer that translates the concept of 'files' and 'directories' into actual disk block allocations. It maintains metadata (sizes, permissions, timestamps), tracks which blocks belong to which files, and handles free space management.

questions.question: Why do many high-performance systems (like Kafka and LSM-tree databases) prefer append-only sequential writes over random writes?
options: Append-only writes are easier to debug
Sequential appends avoid seek penalties, maximize disk throughput, and make crash recovery simpler via log replay
Random writes are not supported by modern file systems
Append-only writes use less disk space
questions.explanation: Sequential appends are the fastest write pattern on both HDDs (no seek) and SSDs (write amplification is minimized). They also simplify crash recovery: you know the last complete record in the log is the recovery point. Kafka achieves millions of messages per second by exploiting sequential I/O.

questions.question: A database server has 64 GB of RAM and a 500 GB dataset. After running for several hours, approximately what percentage of queries might hit the page cache if the working set is 40 GB?
options: Close to 100%, since the 40 GB working set fits entirely in the 64 GB page cache
Exactly 50%, since half the data fits in RAM
0%, because the dataset exceeds RAM size
questions.explanation: The working set — the data actually accessed by queries — is 40 GB, which fits within the 64 GB of available RAM for page caching. After warming up, nearly all queries hit cached pages. The total dataset size (500 GB) matters less than whether the working set fits in memory.

questions.question: An HDD has an average seek time of 8ms and rotational latency of 4ms. For a workload of 1,000 random 4KB reads, approximately how long will it take, and how does this compare to sequential reading of the same 4MB of data?
options: Random: ~12 seconds; Sequential: ~12 seconds (no difference)
Random: ~12 seconds; Sequential: ~25 milliseconds (about 480x faster sequentially)
Random: ~1 second; Sequential: ~1 second
Random: ~120 seconds; Sequential: ~60 seconds
questions.explanation: Each random read costs ~12ms (8ms seek + 4ms rotational latency), so 1,000 reads take ~12 seconds. The same 4MB read sequentially at ~150 MB/s throughput takes about 25ms — roughly 480 times faster. This dramatic difference is why database indexes, log-structured storage, and sequential access patterns exist.

questions.question: A system uses WAL for crash recovery. After a crash, the WAL contains 3 committed transactions and 1 incomplete transaction. What should the recovery process do?
options: Discard the entire WAL and start fresh
Replay the 3 committed transactions to restore consistent state, and discard the incomplete transaction
Replay all 4 transactions including the incomplete one
Restore from the most recent full backup and ignore the WAL
questions.explanation: During WAL recovery, the system replays all fully committed transactions (those with both a begin and commit record in the log) to bring the data files up to date. The incomplete transaction — which lacks a commit record — is rolled back or simply ignored, ensuring the database recovers to a consistent state.
